rationale: A wins because it knows where the trapdoors are and labels them before a reporter does. Its consumer angle, “When the chatbot handles the dispute, who does the consumer appeal to?”, stays inside the supplied facts and turns the risk into a defensible question. B has usable bones, but “Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes” invents a fact the update does not give; that is how a promising pitch becomes a correction waiting to happen.
gaps_in_A: “Klarna automated two-thirds of its chats. The other third got harder.” Strong angle, but the headline states an unproven consequence. The update does not say the remaining human caseload got harder.
“the humans keep a caseload that is now entirely the hard third” overstates the inference. It needs residual-ticket mix and human handle-time data before it can be said that bluntly.
“two-thirds of its support desk automated” is a little too broad. The fact is two-thirds of customer-service chats, not necessarily the whole support desk or support function.
gaps_in_B: “one of the only companies publishing operational numbers” is not in the update. Maybe true, maybe not; in a blind angle set, it is an invented rarity claim.

“Klarna's AI resolves disputes in under two minutes” is the bad miss. The update says average customer-service resolution time fell under two minutes; it does not say disputes are resolved by AI in that time.
“AI head-count reduction” smuggles in causation and job-cut mechanics Klarna refuses to disclose. The facts say hiring froze and headcount fell about 20%, partly through attrition.
“let attrition cut head count 20%” sands off the most important caveat. The update says “partly through attrition,” and the cut-versus-unfilled split is explicitly unknown.
